Rashi on Eruvin 6b:10:1.english: A crooked alleyway - Its two openings open onto the public domain, as in this diagram:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:10:2.english: And they needed doors for it - at its two bends.

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:10:3.english: His ruling is like that of an open-through (mefulash) passage - And here there are two open-through passages (pilushin) of a public domain:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:10:4.english: The halakha follows the first Tanna - That he does not need a door, only a tzurat hapetach [the form of a doorway]:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:14:1.hebrew: בת קול - לקמן בפירקין (עירובין ד' יג:), שיצאה בת קול ואמרה הלכה כבית הלל:
Rashi on Eruvin 6b:14:1.english: Bat kol - Below in this chapter (Eruvin 13b), where a heavenly voice went out and declared that the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:1:1.english: A lechi (side-post) from here - next to the corner of the one house:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:1:2.english: And a jamb on this side - Positioned alongside the far side of that same house, it forms a closure for both ends of the public domain, so one may carry from house to house.

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:2:1.hebrew: ירושלים - רשות הרבים שלה מכוון משער לשער ומפולש, ויש בה דריסת ששים ריבוא ורחב שש עשרה אמה, ואילמלא שנועלין דלתותיה בכל לילה, חייבין עליה בשבת משום רה"ר, אבל נעילת דלתות משויא לה כחצר של רבים, ומערבין את כולה, וכל זמן שלא עירבו, הויא כרמלית ולא מיחייבי עלה, והכי נמי אמרינן בפרק בתרא (ד' קא.) דירושלים כרמלית היא:
Rashi on Eruvin 6b:2:1.english: Jerusalem - Its public domain (reshut harabim) runs straight from gate to gate and is open-ended. It has room for the footfall of six hundred thousand people and is sixteen cubits wide. If its doors were not locked every night, one would be liable for carrying there on Shabbat because of the public domain. But locking its doors makes it like a shared courtyard, and [the residents] join all of it together by an eruv. As long as they have not joined it, it is a karmelit, and one is not liable for carrying there. So too we say in the last chapter (page 101a) that Jerusalem is a karmelit:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:3:1.english: Abuli of Mahoza - The gates of the city face one another, and it had sixty myriads [i.e., 600,000 people]:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:3:2.hebrew: חייבין עליה כו' - אלמא נעילת דלתות בעינן בכל לילה, והכא קתני עושה דלת מכאן ולחי וקורה מכאן לבית הלל:
Rashi on Eruvin 6b:3:2.english: They are obligated to it, etc. - This shows that locking the doors is required every night, and here the mishna teaches: one makes a door on this side, and a lechi (side post) and kora (crossbeam) on that side, according to Beit Hillel:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:6:1.english: Must one lock - That is, a single door.

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:7:1.english: The avulei of Nehardea - These were the heads of alleyways that open out into the public domain:

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:7:2.english: That are buried up to their halves in the dust - Sealed up to half their height in the dust, so a person cannot lock them because of the dust. Taymen is like 'the Philistines buried [them]' (Genesis 26):

Rashi on Eruvin 6b:8:1.english: They were closed (megufot) - Not all of them were open, but rather closed and partly open. Megufot is like the closing of doors (Arakhin ד' יא:).

Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:12:1.hebrew: ומי עבדינן כתרי חומרי - ואם תאמר, ומאי סלקא דעתך השתא, כיון דלא סתרו אהדדי, וכי משום דהלכתא כוותיה בחד דוכתא, יהא הלכה כמותו בכל מקום? ובכמה מקומות קיימא לן כמר בהא וכמר בהא; ויש לומר דלא דמי, דהאי מבוי שרי בצ"ה לכולי עלמא, וליכא מאן דמצריך דלתות:
Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:12:1.english: Do we follow two stringencies? - And if you say: what do you mean now? Since they do not contradict one another, should the halakha follow one of them everywhere merely because the halakha follows him in one place? Yet in several places we hold like this one and like that one. And it may be said that it is not comparable: this alley is permitted with a symbolic doorway (tzurat hapetah) according to all, and there is no one who requires doors.

Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:15:1.hebrew: כאן לאחר בת קול - ואם תאמר, מאי שנא דלא קיימא לן כבת קול דרבי אליעזר דהזהב (ב"מ ד' נט:)? ויש לומר, דהתם לא יצאה אלא לכבודו, כדמוכח התם. ועוד, דהתם היתה כנגד רבים, והתורה אמרה אחרי רבים להטות; אבל הכא, אדרבה, בית הלל הוו רובא, ולא הוצרכו בת קול אלא משום דבית שמאי הוו חריפי טפי. ואם תאמר, אם כן מאי קאמר ר' יהושע, היא דאמר אין משגיחין בבת קול? הלא לא אמר רבי יהושע אלא אבת קול דר"א. וי"ל, דלא בשמים היא, משמע דאין להשגיח כלל בשום בת קול:
Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:15:1.english: Here, after the bat kol - If you say, "Why is it different that we do not follow the bat kol of R. Eliezer in the chapter of HaZahav (Bava Metzia 59b)?" One can answer that there it was issued only for his honor, as is evident there. Moreover, there the bat kol was against the majority, and the Torah says, "to incline after the many" (Exodus 23:2). But here, on the contrary, Beit Hillel were the majority, and a bat kol was needed only because Beit Shammai were sharper. If you say, "If so, what does R. Yehoshua mean, he who says one does not heed a bat kol? Surely R. Yehoshua said only about the bat kol of R. Eliezer!" One can answer that "it is not in heaven" (Deuteronomy 30:12) implies that one should not heed any bat kol at all.

Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:1:1.hebrew: מי שיש לו שני בתים כו' - פי' שתי חצירות, דאין מבוי ניתר בלחי עד שיהו חצירות פתוחות לתוכו, ובתוספתא גרסי' בהדיא ב' חצירות:
Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:1:1.english: One who has two houses, etc. - That is, two courtyards (chatzerot), for an alley cannot be permitted by a lechi (side-post) unless the courtyards open into it. And in the Tosefta we explicitly read “two courtyards.”

Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:2:1.english: And if you would say that it is only because of this that they are not combined, etc. - It implies that [the Gemara] concludes that even with doors they are not combined, and so it is dealing with a full public domain sixteen amot wide. This is difficult: later in this chapter (Eruvin 10) we say that R. Yehuda permitted at most up to thirteen and a third amot. One can answer that initially one would certainly have assumed that R. Yehuda is speaking of a width of sixteen amot. But according to the conclusion, which answers 'How do they combine open alleys?', so too that case of 'more than this' deals with an open alley that is not sixteen amot in width. Thus it is only because of this that they are not combined; with doors they are combined. There is no difficulty from Jerusalem, which is sixteen amot wide. Alternatively, one may say that initially too he knew well that R. Yehuda only permitted up to thirteen and a third amot, and nevertheless it is a full public domain, for example, where one public domain lies on one side of the alley and is sixteen amot wide, and people walk the length of the public domain by way of the alley (1): Now, even in an alley that is not sixteen amot wide, it is a full public domain, since on both sides of the alley together the width is sixteen amot, like [the case of] between the pillars, which, as stated in the first chapter of Shabbat (Shabbat 7), is a public domain even though it is not sixteen amot. Even according to the one who holds there that between the pillars is a karmelit, that is because they are pillars not opposite one another and their use is not convenient, and it is unlike open alleys, for there the public domain does not pass through the alley, but two public domains pass alongside the openings (2): And it must be explained accordingly: although according to R. Yehuda a lechi and koreh are effective rabbinically for a width of thirteen but not for a width of sixteen, he concedes that biblically there is no distinction between thirteen and sixteen, and he holds that two walls are required biblically. Therefore the question is raised from Jerusalem, even though it is sixteen amot wide, since one is liable there for carrying in a public domain by biblical law; the same applies to a width of thirteen, since biblically there is no distinction. And if you say: since R. Yehuda holds that two walls are required biblically, why must the baraita in the first chapter of Shabbat (Shabbat 6) teach, 'This is a full private domain: a trench ten tefachim deep and four [tefachim] wide, etc.,' to exclude R. Yehuda's 'more than this'? Rather, since it is taught at the outset, 'What is a public domain? Streets, squares, and open alleys,' we can clearly understand that it serves to exclude R. Yehuda, for in his view open alleys are not a public domain since they have two walls. And one may answer: had it been taught only from the beginning, I would have thought that R. Yehuda's reason is not two walls but that he holds a lechi and koreh count as a wall, and there is someone in this chapter who holds this. Therefore it was necessary to teach 'This is a full private domain,' to exclude R. Yehuda, meaning that it is not a private domain, since a lechi and koreh are not considered a wall.

Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:2:2.hebrew: והאמר רבה כו' - פ"ה דפריך אמאי דשרינן לחי וקורה מצד אחד, ומדמצריך לנעילת דלת, אינו נראה לו שהיה מקשה לו, דאיכא לאוקומא נמי בננעלת. ואם תאמר, כיון דיש לו ב' מחיצות ושלישית בננעלת, הוי ג' מחיצות? ולקמן אמר דלכל היותר לב"ה שלש מחיצות דאורייתא. ויש לומר לפירושו, דהיינו דווקא היכא דאיכא ג' מחיצות גמורות הוו דאורייתא; אבל הכא, דשלישית ע"י דלת, רביעית נמי צריך דלת. ולר"י נראה דפריך משום דמשמע ליה דב"ה לא בעי נעילה, וכן אמר בסמוך דבברייתא לא מפרש בדברי ב"ה נעילה כמו בדברי ב"ש. וא"ת, והיכי פריך מר' יוחנן דאמר בפרק ב' דהוי אליבא דרבי יהודה, דאמר אתו רבים ומבטלי מחיצתא, ופליגי עליה התם רבנן? ויש לומר דפריך, כי היכי דלר' יהודה בשם ד' מחיצות דלא חשיבי ליה מצריך נעילה, הכי נמי ב' מחיצות דלא חשיבי לרבנן יהיה צריך נעילה. וכן משמע בפרק שני (ד' כב.) דשתי מחיצות לרבנן כשם ד' מחיצות לרבי יהודה:
Tosafot on Eruvin 6b:2:2.english: And Rava said, etc. - The explanation is that [the Gemara] objects: why does it permit a lechi and a beam on one side, when Rava requires a locked door? It does not seem to [Tosafot] that the Gemara would raise this objection, since the case can also be established where the door is locked. But if you say: since [the enclosure] has two walls and the third is formed by a locked door, does it not count as three walls? And later the Gemara says that according to Beit Hillel, at most three walls are required by Torah law. One may explain his view that this applies only where there are three complete walls, which are Torah-law; but here, where the third is formed by means of a door, a fourth also requires a door. In the view of R. Yitzchak, it seems the Gemara objects because it understood that Beit Hillel do not require locking, and so it says in the following passage that in the baraita, Beit Hillel's words do not specify locking as Beit Shammai's do. And if you ask: how can [the Gemara] object from R. Yochanan, who said in chapter two that [his ruling] follows R. Yehuda, who said that when many people come and nullify a partition, and the Sages disagree with him there? One may say that the Gemara objects as follows: just as, according to R. Yehuda, a structure with four walls that he does not count as walls requires locking, so too a structure with two walls that the Sages do not count should require locking. And this is indicated in chapter two (Eruvin 22a) that two walls according to the Sages are like four walls according to R. Yehuda:
